options.description: The code to analyse: a .jar or .zip, a single .class file, or a folder of classes.
More jars or folders whose classes are interpreted alongside the sample, such as libraries it expects to find.
What to run, in order. Empty means the main method named in the sample's manifest.
main runs the main method; method runs one named method; clinit-sweep runs every class's start-up code, which makes most obfuscators decrypt their hidden text without running the program.
The class to run, with dots or slashes. For main it defaults to the manifest's Main-Class.
The method to run. Required when type is method.
The method's JVM descriptor, such as (Ljava/lang/String;)V. Needed only when the method name is overloaded.
For main: the program arguments. For method: one value per parameter.
For clinit-sweep: class-name patterns to include. Empty means every class.
Budgets that end a run with a named reason instead of letting it hang.
Bytecode instructions the run may execute before it ends with outcome instruction-limit.
Real seconds the run may take before it ends with outcome timeout.
How deep the sample's calls may nest before it gets a StackOverflowError, as on a real JVM.
Sleeps one thread may perform. Beacon loops sleep for ever, so this is what ends them.
Threads, timers and background jobs one run may start.
Events kept per category. Further events are counted but not stored.
Total bytes the sample may write to the pretend disk.
The pretend machine the sample believes it is running on.
The operating system to pretend to be. It decides path style and system properties.
The user name the sample sees.
The computer name the sample sees.
Where the sample believes it is stored. Droppers copy or restart themselves from here.
Extra or changed Java system properties.
Extra or changed environment variables.
Files that exist on the pretend disk before the run starts.
Where the file is on the pretend disk.
The file's content as text.
The file's content as base64, for binary files.
A real file on this computer whose content the pretend file has.
Folders that exist on the pretend disk before the run starts.
When the pretend clock starts, as an ISO-8601 time such as 2024-03-01T09:00:00Z. Empty means now.
Seed for random numbers the sample does not seed itself, so that runs are repeatable. Empty means truly random.
The simulated network. Nothing is ever really sent.
respond: connections succeed and get the answers set here or an empty one. offline: connections fail as on an unplugged computer.
Answers for web requests. The first rule whose pattern matches the address is used.
A regular expression searched for in the full web address. Required.
The HTTP status code of the answer.
Headers of the answer.
The answer's body as text.
The answer's body as base64, for binary data.
A real file on this computer whose content is the answer's body.
Data sent back on raw network connections. The first matching rule is used.
A regular expression matched against host:port. Required.
Data sent back, as text.
Data sent back, as base64.
A real file on this computer whose content is sent back.
Host names and the addresses they look up to. Other names get the default address.
The address every host name not listed under dns looks up to.
The pretend computer's own network address.
The pretend computer's network card address. Sandbox checks often look at it.
Made-up results for programs the sample tries to start. Nothing is ever really started.
A regular expression searched for in the command line. Required.
What the pretend program prints.
What the pretend program prints as errors.
The pretend program's exit code.
Changes to which real JDK calls the sample may make.
JDK members to allow in addition to the built-in list. Allow only code with no effect outside the process.
JDK members to refuse even though the built-in list allows them.
What a refused JDK call does. phantom: record it and give back a harmless value so the run continues. throw: give the sample a SecurityException. abort: end the run.
Overrides for chosen methods in the sample, applied before they run.
Which methods, as a pattern such as com/example/Checks.isSandbox()Z; * matches anything. Required.
return: skip the method and give back value. skip: do nothing. throw: raise the exception class named in value. trace: run it normally and record its calls.
For return: the value to give back. For throw: the exception class name.
What to record beyond the sample's behaviour.
Which methods have the text they return recorded. static catches decryption helpers without flooding the report; all includes instance methods; none turns it off.
Patterns of methods whose calls, arguments and results are recorded.
Patterns of methods recorded instruction by instruction in the trace. Very verbose.
Record every call into the real JDK. Verbose; useful when extending the allow-list.
How the sample's threads are scheduled. They take turns; only one runs at a time.
deferred: a new thread first runs when the current one waits or uses up its turn. inline: a new thread runs at once.
How many times a repeating timer or scheduled job is run.
Whether the sample's shutdown code runs at the end.
Where and how results are written.
The folder for the report, trace and saved files.
Save every class the sample creates while running, in defined-classes/.
Save every file the sample writes, in dropped/.
What the run command prints. text: a readable summary. json: the report. quiet: nothing.
Settings for plugins, by plugin id. A plugin runs only if it has an entry here.
